name: Magnesium threonate
lead: Magnesium L-threonate is a salt of magnesium and threonic acid, a metabolite of vitamin C, sold as an oral dietary supplement under names such as Magtein. It is marketed as a form of magnesium intended to raise magnesium levels in the brain, and in appearance and recovery communities it is taken mainly in the evening for sleep, calm and cognition rather than for any direct effect on facial or bodily features.

The idea behind the product comes from a 2010 rat study in which elevated brain magnesium was associated with improved learning and memory, described in a commentary in Neuron [2]. Human evidence is limited: a few small trials have been registered or completed in older adults, people with dementia, people with ADHD and, more recently, healthy adults and athletes [4][5][6][7], but the registry entries reviewed here do not report results.

Magnesium in general is an established nutrient, and excess oral magnesium most commonly causes diarrhea [1]. Whether the threonate form delivers more magnesium to the brain than other forms, or improves sleep in humans, has not been established in the published sources reviewed for this article.

paras: Magnesium L-threonate is sold for memory, mood, stress and sleep. In looksmaxxing and recovery circles it is usually added to bedtime supplement routines, on the premise that better sleep supports skin, energy and general appearance.

Magnesium ions block the NMDA-type glutamate receptor channel and reduce nerve cell activity at high concentrations [1]. A 2010 commentary on rat experiments described oral magnesium threonate as raising brain magnesium and increasing hippocampal NR2B expression and synapse density, accompanied by better cognition in young and old rats over 12 to 24 days [2]. Later rodent work has also studied the compound, for example a 2023 preprint reporting changes in the urine proteome of rats after short-term intake [3]. A 2016 review of magnesium in the nervous system noted a long-standing interest in neuroprotective roles but that translation to clinical use has been difficult [8].

Human research on the threonate form is sparse and mostly registered rather than published. A trial of Magtein in older adults, started in 2012, enrolled 50 participants with mood and anxiety as listed conditions [4]. Small trials registered in people with dementia (17 participants) [5] and ADHD (20 participants) [6] have been completed. Newer registered studies examine sleep, recovery and performance in healthy adults, collegiate athletes, people after knee arthroplasty and menopausal women [7][9][10][11][12]. The registry entries do not provide published results, so effect sizes are not available from these sources.

For magnesium supplements generally, diarrhea is the most common symptom of excess oral intake, poisoning is very rare with normal kidney function, and high blood magnesium usually results from kidney dysfunction [1]. The US tolerable upper intake level for supplemental magnesium is 350 mg per day and the European limit is 250 mg per day, according to Wikipedia [1]. Safety data specific to the threonate form are limited in the sources reviewed.

It is commonly listed alongside apigenin and theanine in bedtime stacks; see the entry on the Huberman sleep stack. Dietary supplements as a category are not approved by regulators for treating conditions before sale.

timeline.event: Rat study on elevated brain magnesium and cognition with magnesium threonate discussed in Neuron [2].
Trial of Magtein in older adults begins [4].
Pilot trial in people with dementia begins [5].
Several sleep and recovery trials in healthy adults and athletes are registered [7][9][10].

lore.intro: Magnesium threonate is discussed as the 'brain' form of magnesium and a common bedtime addition in sleep stacks.

claims.claim: Threonate crosses into the brain better than other magnesium forms
claims.believers: Supplement marketers and stack advocates say the threonate salt is specifically able to raise brain magnesium, unlike oxide or citrate.
claims.experts: The supporting data cited most often come from rat experiments described in a 2010 commentary [2]; no published human study in the sources reviewed has measured brain magnesium after the supplement.

claims.believers: Users report deeper or calmer sleep when taking it in the evening.
claims.experts: Human sleep trials are registered but have no published results in the sources reviewed [7][9][12].

card.summary: A brain-targeted magnesium salt taken at night for sleep; the idea rests on rat data and human proof is thin.
card.note: Human sleep trials are registered but results are not published in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Magnesium threonate is a supplement form of magnesium sold as being able to raise magnesium in the brain. People in recovery and sleep communities add it to bedtime routines for calm, sleep and focus.

The key study behind it was in rats; human trials exist mostly as registrations without published results.
quick.mechanism: Magnesium ions dampen NMDA receptor activity, and rat work described by a Neuron commentary linked raised brain magnesium to more synapses and better cognition.
quick.risks: Excess oral magnesium most often causes diarrhea, and high blood levels mostly occur with kidney dysfunction. It is sold as a dietary supplement; threonate-specific safety data are limited.
